analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes the government's foreign-surveillance program for five years while restricting FBI searches of Americans' communications.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2024 and referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees, where it sat with no further action and no cosponsors until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend for five years Section 702 of FISA — the program under which the government collects foreign communications, sometimes sweeping in Americans' messages and calls. It would also add rules aimed at the FBI's use of that data: FBI personnel would need a supervisor's or lawyer's approval before searching for an American's communications, politically sensitive searches (of officials, candidates, journalists) would need the Deputy Director's sign-off, and searches aimed only at finding evidence of a crime would be barred. It would also require sworn statements in surveillance applications, ban relying on uncorroborated political or press material, mandate audits and discipline for improper searching, and raise penalties for FISA violations. The bill never received any action after being referred to two House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, ordinary Americans would gain tighter legal limits on FBI searches of their communications collected without a warrant, including searches of members of Congress, candidates, and journalists, plus annual public reporting on how often such searches happen. Intelligence agency employees who mishandle surveillance data would face new penalties. The same law would also preserve the underlying foreign-surveillance program's access to communications data for five years.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans whose communications get swept up in surveillance

how_it_helps.text: Bars FBI personnel from searching the contents of Americans' communications collected under Section 702 without prior approval from a supervisor or attorney, with an exception only when a query might stop a threat to life or serious bodily harm.

Prohibits FBI queries solely designed to find and extract evidence of a crime, and restricts the FBI from ingesting unminimized communications about Americans unless the person is relevant to an open national security investigation.

Requires the FBI Deputy Director to personally approve queries naming elected officials, candidates, political organizations, or media organizations, and bars political appointees from the approval process.

Requires sworn factual statements in surveillance applications, bans reliance on uncorroborated political-organization or press material, and requires disclosure of information that might undermine the application — responses to documented past FBI application errors.

Mandates Justice Department audits of every FBI U.S.-person query, annual Inspector General reporting on querying compliance, escalating discipline for noncompliant searching including zero tolerance for willful misconduct, and accountability up to removal for officials who mislead the surveillance court.
Raises civil damages for surveillance violations to at least $10,000 per person and extends contempt power over the surveillance courts, giving violations of the law financial and legal consequences.

analysis.who_pays: The FBI and other intelligence agencies would bear the cost: new approval requirements, mandatory query audits, discipline for noncompliant searching, expanded criminal and civil penalties, and required reports to Congress and the public.

drawbacks.text: By reauthorizing Title VII of FISA for five years, the bill would keep the underlying bulk electronic-surveillance program in place for at least that long, even as it restricts how FBI can search what is collected.

The FBI remains exempt from the criminal-query prohibition for 'threat to life or serious bodily harm' cases and for litigation-related queries, and the FISA Court can waive the detailed querying safeguards if it finds alternative procedures work as well.

Many of the bill's mechanisms are audits, reports, and certifications to Congress rather than rights enforceable by individuals, so a person who believes their communications were searched improperly would gain little they could act on directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs real checks on FBI searches of Americans' communications with a five-year extension of the underlying collection power itself, which is the main cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge. The strongest objection is that the abuses it addresses were largely already the subject of FISA Court-ordered fixes; the bill would have written them into statute but also locked in the program. Weighing both, the privacy gains are concrete but modest, and the reauthorization they were attached to is substantial.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees, where no one scheduled any action on it, and it died there when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 13, 2024 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without any action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence agencies and anyone opposed to statutory limits on FBI querying benefit from the bill's death, since the restrictions it contained were never enacted in this form.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Intelligence agencies and backers of the surveillance status quo

for.name: House Judiciary and Intelligence Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or committee actions ever occurred, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown; the bill had zero cosponsors.

industries.industry: FBI and other intelligence agencies (NSA, CIA)
industries.note: The bill would keep the Section 702 collection program authorized for five more years while imposing statutory pre-approval requirements, mandatory audits, personnel discipline, and new criminal and civil penalties on FBI querying and disclosure practices.

industries.industry: Telecommunications and technology companies serving as Section 702 providers
industries.note: Reauthorization preserves the legal framework requiring these companies to assist government surveillance; the bill does not address their role directly.
